set1.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set1.q: A 45-year-old man's father has been in a coma for a week. The son asks how coma differs from very deep sleep. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: A sleeper can be roused; a person in coma cannot

Correct. Both sleep and coma are states of unconsciousness. The difference is arousal: sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli, and coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused by stimuli, however deep the sleep is.
Coma is the deepest stage of sleep

The deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, stage N3, is still sleep: more difficult to arouse, yet arousable by stimuli. Tell: coma is not a sleep stage at all; it is defined by the inability to be aroused, whatever the depth.
A sleeper is conscious; a person in coma is not

Sleep is unconsciousness too; a sleeper is not conscious. Tell: both states are unconsciousness, and what separates them is whether stimuli can arouse the person, which is possible in sleep and not in coma.
Coma shows slower brain waves than sleep

Slow, high-voltage delta waves occur in very deep sleep as well as in serious organic brain disease, so slow waves do not mark the boundary between sleep and coma. Tell: the definitions turn on arousal, not on wave speed.

set1.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set1.q: A 28-year-old woman in a sleep laboratory has passed beyond drowsy, light sleep. She is now less responsive, her heart rate and temperature are falling, and her electroencephalogram shows theta waves. Which stage is she in?
opts: Stage N1 also shows theta waves, but it is the drowsy transition from wakefulness into light sleep. Tell: she has passed beyond drowsy, light sleep and her heart rate and temperature are falling, which marks stage N2.
ruled out by a stated finding

Stage N3, the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, shows delta waves, below 3.5 cycles per second. Tell: her tracing shows theta waves together with falling heart rate and temperature, which fits stage N2 rather than stage N3.

Rapid eye movement sleep shows a mixed, low-voltage, beta-like tracing with sawtooth waves, and its heart rate is irregular. Tell: theta waves with a steady fall in heart rate and temperature point to stage N2.

Correct. Stage N2 is less responsive, deeper sleep in which heart rate and temperature decrease, and its electroencephalogram shows theta waves. She has moved past the drowsy, light sleep of stage N1 but does not show the delta waves of stage N3.

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: A 22-year-old student asks how long one complete sleep cycle lasts. Which answer is accurate?
opts: This is closer to the length of a single rapid eye movement episode, which lasts 5 to 30 minutes, than to a whole cycle. Tell: a cycle holds non-rapid eye movement sleep as well as the rapid eye movement episode and runs 90 to 120 minutes.

Cycles this short would fit 8 to 10 into an 8-hour night, but an average night holds 4 to 5. Tell: rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes, which marks the length of a cycle at 90 to 120 minutes.

Correct. Each sleep cycle lasts 90 to 120 minutes, and an average 8 hours of sleep holds 4 to 5 of them. Within each cycle non-rapid eye movement sleep is followed by a rapid eye movement episode, and those episodes recur about every 90 minutes.

At 3 to 4 hours per cycle, an 8-hour night would hold only 2 to 3 cycles rather than 4 to 5. Tell: each cycle runs 90 to 120 minutes, about the interval between one rapid eye movement episode and the next.

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: A 20-year-old student plans to sleep 3 hours a night for the 4 nights before an exam, reasoning that nobody knows what sleep is for anyway. What should he be told?
opts: Short nights can impair his thinking

Correct. Sleep restriction over a few days can decrease cognitive and physical performance, productivity and health, and the functions of sleep include cognition and the facilitation of learning or memory. Four nights of 3 hours is restriction over a few days, so his studying could backfire.
Sleep's role is unknown, so cutting it is safe

Researchers have limited understanding of why sleep is essential, but its importance is not in doubt: restriction over a few days already decreases performance. Tell: unknown mechanisms do not mean no effect.
Harm needs months of short sleep

Restriction over a few days is enough to decrease cognitive and physical performance, productivity and health. Tell: 4 short nights fall within that window, so harm is expected well before months have passed.
Short sleep mainly costs physical strength

Restriction lowers physical performance, but it lowers cognitive performance too, and sleep supports cognition and learning or memory. Tell: for exam preparation, the cognitive cost is the one that matters, and it is part of the expected effect.

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: A 24-year-old student has been awake and studying for 20 hours and finally dozes off at his desk. Which proposed mechanism explains his transition from wakefulness to sleep?
opts: Positive feedback between the reticular nuclei and the cortex sustains wakefulness, and it fades rather than strengthens as sleep approaches. Tell: strengthening that loop would keep him awake; its fading lets the sleep-promoting centers take over.
Release of reticular nuclei from inhibition

Release of the mesencephalic and upper pontile reticular activating nuclei from inhibition is the proposed start of wakefulness, when the sleep centers are not activated. Tell: release from inhibition wakes the brain; fatigue of those neurons lets sleep in.

Increased parasympathetic tone describes the body during non-rapid eye movement sleep, with low blood pressure and slow heart rate. Tell: it is a feature of sleep once it has begun, while the proposed trigger for the transition is fatigue of the activating system.

Correct. After the brain has remained active for many hours, neurons in the activating system become fatigued, the positive feedback cycle between the mesencephalic reticular nuclei and the cerebral cortex fades, and the sleep-promoting centers take over. Twenty hours of studying fits that fatigue.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 19, 18, 14

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: A 37-year-old woman believes that sleep matters for the brain and nothing else. Which statement about the physiological effects of sleep is accurate?
opts: The effects of sleep are physiological, on the nervous system and on other body systems, including blood pressure, heart rate, breathing and metabolic rate. Tell: a measurable 10 to 30% fall in these values during non-rapid eye movement sleep is not psychological.
It affects brain and body systems

Correct. Sleep has two major types of physiological effects: effects on the nervous system and effects on the other functional systems of the body. Its functions span both, from neural maturation and cognition to conservation of metabolic energy, so its importance is not limited to the brain.

That leaves out half of the picture: sleep also has effects on other functional systems of the body, such as the fall in blood pressure, heart rate and metabolic rate in non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: there are two types of effects, nervous system and body.

Muscle tone does change in sleep, being very depressed in rapid eye movement sleep, but the two major types of effects are on the nervous system and on the other functional systems. Tell: the brain is one of the two targets, not left out.

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: A 24-year-old competitive cyclist has cut her sleep to 5 hours a night for the 4 nights before a race. Which effect on her race performance is expected?
opts: Correct. Sleep restriction over a few days can decrease physical as well as cognitive performance, along with productivity and health. Four nights of 5 hours before her race is restriction over a few days, so her physical performance is expected to fall.

Trading sleep for training time does not raise endurance; restriction over a few days decreases physical performance. Tell: the effects of restriction run downward, in physical and cognitive performance alike.
No change after so few nights
A few nights are enough: sleep restriction over a few days can already decrease physical and cognitive performance. Tell: 4 short nights is within that window, so an effect on her race is expected.
Faster times from a lower heart rate

The slow heart rate of non-rapid eye movement sleep is a change during sleep itself, not a racing benefit of sleeping less. Tell: cutting sleep lowers physical performance; it does not borrow the slowing of deep sleep.

set1.q: A 30-year-old man's overnight recording shows a stretch of irregular, high-frequency, low-voltage waves, and the reviewer cannot tell from the electroencephalogram alone whether he is awake and active or in rapid eye movement sleep. Which additional finding best settles the question?
opts: Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep is often difficult to tell apart from being awake and active on the electroencephalogram, because both show irregular, high-frequency waves. The difference is in the muscles: rapid eye movement sleep pairs the waking-like tracing with atonia of the voluntary muscles, sparing the eyes and diaphragm.

A steady fall in heart rate marks non-rapid eye movement sleep, while in rapid eye movement sleep the heart rate becomes irregular. Tell: the question is awake versus rapid eye movement sleep, and the feature that separates them is atonia of the voluntary muscles.

Delta waves mark stage N3, the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, and belong to neither of the two states in question. Tell: both candidates have fast tracings, so looking for slow waves cannot separate them, while muscle atonia can.

Alert wakefulness and rapid eye movement sleep both show fast, irregular, beta-like waves, so the frequency cannot separate them, as the reviewer has already found. Tell: the waves look alike; atonia on the muscle leads marks rapid eye movement sleep.

set1.q: A 35-year-old man's 8-hour sleep recording is scored stage by stage. Which stage takes up the largest share of his total sleep time?
opts: Stage N3 is the deepest, most restful non-rapid eye movement stage, and it decreases with age. Tell: depth is not duration; the stage that is the longest by total duration and fills the majority of the cycle is stage N2.

Stage N1 is the brief, drowsy transition from wakefulness into light sleep. Tell: a transition stage does not make up the bulk of the night; stage N2 is the majority of the sleep cycle and the longest stage by total duration.

Correct. Stage N2 makes up the majority of the sleep cycle and is the longest stage by total duration. Rapid eye movement sleep fills about 25% of a young adult's sleep, and stage N2 outlasts both the brief drowsy stage N1 and the deep stage N3, so it holds the largest share of his night.

Rapid eye movement sleep occupies about 25% of a young adult's sleep time, roughly a quarter of the night. Tell: the stage that makes up the majority of the sleep cycle and the longest by total duration is stage N2, not the dream state.

set1.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set1.q: A 40-year-old man rests quietly with his eyes closed during an electroencephalogram. At what frequency should his dominant rhythm run?
opts: This is the delta range, found in very deep sleep, infancy and serious organic brain disease. Tell: he is an awake adult at quiet rest, whose rhythm is alpha at 8 to 13 per second, not the slow waves of deep sleep.

This is the theta range, seen in children's parietal and temporal regions, during emotional stress in some adults, and in brain disorders. Tell: a calm adult resting with his eyes closed shows alpha at 8 to 13 per second.

Correct. An awake adult in a quiet, resting state, such as resting with the eyes closed, shows alpha waves: rhythmical waves at 8 to 13 cycles per second, most intense over the occipital region. Alpha waves are found in almost all healthy adults in this state.

This is the beta range, which comes with alertness and active processing, as when the eyes are open or attention is focused on a task. Tell: resting with the eyes closed brings alpha at 8 to 13 per second instead.

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: A 23-year-old man asks why trivial details of his day seem to fade after a night's sleep while what mattered stays. Which function of sleep explains this?
opts: Neural maturation is a function of sleep that concerns the maturing of the nervous system, not the pruning of a day's trivia. Tell: forgetting unimportant information that might clutter the network is targeted erasure of synapses.

Correct. One function of sleep is targeted erasure of synapses to forget unimportant information that might otherwise clutter the synaptic network. Losing trivial details while keeping what matters fits that function, which works alongside sleep's facilitation of learning or memory.
That function helps him keep information, the opposite of losing it. Tell: the fading of unimportant details is the work of targeted erasure of synapses, which keeps the synaptic network uncluttered.

Sleep clears metabolic waste products generated by neural activity in the awake brain; that removes chemical by-products, not information. Tell: forgetting trivia on purpose is targeted erasure of synapses, not waste clearance.

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: A 25-year-old man falls asleep at the start of an overnight sleep study. About how long after he falls asleep is his first rapid eye movement period expected?
opts: Ten minutes in, the sleeper is still descending through the non-rapid eye movement stages; in a typical night the first rapid eye movement period comes at the end of the first cycle. Tell: rapid eye movement sleep closes a 90- to 120-minute cycle; it does not open the night.

At about 30 minutes a typical night shows deepening non-rapid eye movement sleep, not rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: 30 minutes is the upper end of one rapid eye movement episode's length (5 to 30 minutes), not the wait before the first one.

Correct. Sleep begins in non-rapid eye movement sleep, and in a typical night the first rapid eye movement period closes the first cycle, between 1 and 2 hours in. Rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes, and each cycle lasts 90 to 120 minutes.

Four hours in, a typical night has already held two rapid eye movement periods, so waiting that long would skip the first two cycles. Tell: rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes, so the first comes about 90 minutes in.

set1.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set1.q: A 29-year-old man lies relaxed with his eyes closed while his electroencephalogram shows a steady alpha rhythm. The study next calls for a recording of his beta waves. What should he be asked to do?
opts: Emotional stress, especially disappointment and frustration, brings theta waves at 4 to 7 per second in some adults. Tell: beta comes from directed mental activity, not from upset, which would slow the tracing instead.
Focus on a specific mental task

Correct. When an awake person's attention is directed to a specific type of mental activity, alpha waves stop and are replaced by beta waves, faster than 14 cycles per second, asynchronous and low voltage, recorded mainly from the frontal and parietal regions.
Keep resting with his eyes closed

Quiet rest with the eyes closed is what produces his alpha rhythm, so continuing it keeps alpha on the tracing. Tell: beta waves need alertness and active processing of information, not continued rest.

Drifting into sleep slows the tracing: the frequency becomes progressively slower as sleep deepens. Tell: beta waves come with alert, active processing, so he must be engaged with a task rather than drowsy.

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: A 74-year-old woman says she no longer sleeps as deeply as she did in her twenties. Which sleep stage can she be told decreases with age?
opts: Stage N2 is the longest stage by total duration, a less responsive, deeper sleep but not the deepest. Tell: losing the deepest sleep with age is a loss of stage N3, the stage that decreases with age.
Stage N1 is the drowsy, light transition from wakefulness. Tell: a light stage cannot explain losing deep sleep; the deepest stage, stage N3, is the one that decreases with age.

Correct. Stage N3, the deep, restful, deepest non-rapid eye movement stage with delta waves, decreases with age. Her sense that her sleep is less deep than it was in her twenties fits a smaller share of stage N3 sleep.

Rapid eye movement sleep is not restful or deep, so it cannot account for a loss of deep sleep. Tell: the deep, restful stage that decreases with age is stage N3, the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage.

set1.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set1.q: A 32-year-old man has rhythmical alpha waves on his electroencephalogram while resting with his eyes closed. When he opens his eyes, the tracing flattens into faster, low-voltage activity. Which waveform has replaced the alpha waves?
opts: Correct. With the eyes closed and relaxed, an awake adult shows alpha waves; with the eyes open the person is alert and active, which brings beta waves, fast and low voltage. On the tracing, alpha flattens into this faster, low-voltage activity when the eyes open and returns when they close.

Theta waves run at 4 to 7 cycles per second, slower than alpha, and appear with emotional stress in some adults or in brain disorders. Tell: opening the eyes made his tracing faster, which points to beta, not to a slower wave.

Delta waves are slow and high voltage, often 2 to 4 times taller than other brain waves, and belong to very deep sleep, infancy and organic brain disease. Tell: his tracing became faster and lower in voltage, the opposite of delta.

Sawtooth waves appear in the mixed, low-voltage tracing of rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: he is awake with his eyes open, and the awake, eyes-open state is marked by beta waves, not by a feature of a sleep stage.

set1.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set1.q: A 78-year-old woman in a nursing home is found in bed with her eyes closed and does not answer when an aide walks into the room. Which step best distinguishes sleep from coma in her?
opts: Look for delta waves on an electroencephalogram

Delta waves occur in very deep sleep as well as in persons with serious organic brain disease, so finding them would not separate sleep from coma. Tell: the definitions differ by arousability, and a stimulus tests that directly at the bedside.
Watch her eyes for rapid movements

Rapid eye movements mark rapid eye movement sleep, but a sleeper in non-rapid eye movement sleep does not show them, so their absence would not mean coma. Tell: the test that defines the difference is whether a stimulus wakes her.

Breathing slows in non-rapid eye movement sleep and turns irregular in rapid eye movement sleep, so a rate describes the stage of sleep rather than separating sleep from coma. Tell: arousal to a stimulus is the deciding test.
Apply a stimulus and watch for arousal

Correct. Sleep and coma are both unconsciousness; what separates them is whether stimuli can arouse the person. Calling her loudly or touching her and watching whether she wakes answers the question directly: arousal means sleep, and no arousal to stimuli means coma.

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: A 46-year-old woman asks what sleep does about the by-products her brain makes while she is awake and thinking. Which function answers her?
opts: Synaptic erasure removes unimportant information that might clutter the synaptic network, not chemical by-products. Tell: the by-products of neural activity in the awake brain are cleared as metabolic waste.

Overall brain metabolism can rise by as much as 20% in rapid eye movement sleep, which is a feature of that stage, not a function that removes by-products. Tell: removal is clearance of metabolic waste.

Correct. One function of sleep is clearance of metabolic waste products generated by neural activity in the awake brain. Her question about the by-products of her brain's waking activity is answered by that clearance function.

Energy conservation is a separate function of sleep, and it concerns saving energy rather than removing anything. Tell: removing the by-products of waking neural activity is clearance of metabolic waste, not conservation of energy.

set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with a degenerative brain disorder has an electroencephalogram while awake and calm. It shows waves at 4 to 7 cycles per second. Which explanation best fits these waves?
opts: Very deep sleep brings delta waves, below 3.5 cycles per second, and she is awake. Tell: her waves are theta, faster than delta, and her degenerative brain disorder is the setting that produces them.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Waves at 4 to 7 cycles per second are theta waves, which occur in many brain disorders, especially degenerative brain states. In a calm, awake adult with a known degenerative brain disorder, that disorder best explains them.

Theta waves do appear during emotional stress in some adults, especially with disappointment and frustration, but she is calm. Tell: in a calm adult with a degenerative brain disorder, the disorder explains the theta waves.
ruled out by a stated finding

A calm, relaxed adult at quiet rest shows alpha waves at 8 to 13 cycles per second, not theta. Tell: 4 to 7 per second is theta, which in an adult signals emotional stress or a brain disorder, not a normal resting rhythm.

Each cycle of a typical night ends in a rapid eye movement period, and the last one leads into waking; people can awaken spontaneously in the morning during rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: late cycles hold longer rapid eye movement periods, not none.

Each cycle lasts 90 to 120 minutes through the night. Tell: 30 minutes is the upper length of one rapid eye movement episode (5 to 30 minutes), not of a whole cycle, and the late cycles are not shortened to that.
A longer rapid eye movement period

Correct. Across a typical night, rapid eye movement periods grow longer in the later cycles, while the deepest non-rapid eye movement sleep falls in the first cycles. This fits rapid eye movement episodes lengthening as the sleeper becomes more rested.

Stage N1 is the brief, drowsy transition from wakefulness into light sleep. Tell: the sleep that follows more than 24 hours awake is deep and extremely restful, which is deep non-rapid eye movement sleep, not light sleep.

Quiet wakefulness is a relaxed, awake state with alpha waves, and alpha waves disappear during deep sleep. Tell: he has fallen asleep, and the first hour after a sleepless night is deep sleep, so the resting awake rhythm is gone.

Alpha waves are the usual resting rhythm of healthy adults, found in almost all of them, not in a minority. Tell: a quiet, resting, healthy adult such as this man is exactly the person in whom alpha waves are expected.

The wave tied to children is theta, at 4 to 7 cycles per second over the parietal and temporal regions. Tell: alpha belongs to healthy adults at quiet rest, almost all of whom show it, so his age fits alpha.
Found in almost all of them

set1.q: A 28-year-old woman wakes on her own at the end of a full night's sleep, recalling a vivid dream. From which sleep stage did she probably wake?

set1.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set1.q: A 20-year-old college student is slumped over a library desk with his eyes closed. A friend says his name quietly and he does not respond, but when the friend shakes his arm he wakes and starts talking. Which finding shows he was asleep rather than in a coma?
opts: Closed eyes say nothing about arousability, and arousability is the feature the definitions of sleep and coma turn on. Tell: both states are unconsciousness; what separates them is whether a stimulus can rouse the person, and the shake did.

Lying still describes his unconscious state, not which kind it was, since both sleep and coma are unconsciousness. Tell: his posture cannot decide it; being roused by the shake of his arm places him in sleep rather than coma.
He woke when his arm was shaken

Correct. Sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli; coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused. Waking when his arm was shaken shows he was arousable, so he was asleep, even though a quieter stimulus had failed first.

Not answering a quiet voice shows that he was unconscious, which is true of sleep and coma alike, so it cannot separate them. Tell: the deciding finding is that a stronger stimulus, the shake, did rouse him, which is what makes it sleep.

set1.q: A 33-year-old woman's partner notices that late in the night her eyes dart rapidly under closed lids, her breathing becomes irregular and her fingers twitch. When woken, she describes a vivid dream. Which stage was she in?

Stage N3 is deep, restful non-rapid eye movement sleep, with slow heart rate, decreased breathing and less vivid dreams. Tell: darting eyes, irregular breathing and a vivid dream mark rapid eye movement sleep, not the deepest non-rapid stage.

Stage N2 is deeper non-rapid eye movement sleep with heart rate and temperature falling, and non-rapid eye movement dreams are less vivid and often not remembered. Tell: irregular breathing and darting eyes are rapid eye movement features.

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: A 25-year-old woman has been awake and active for many hours, and the feedback loop between her reticular nuclei and her cerebral cortex is fading. Which centers are proposed to take over at this point?
opts: These areas are inhibited during rapid eye movement sleep to produce atonia; they do not start sleep. Tell: the transition from wakefulness into sleep is handed to the sleep-promoting centers once the activating system fatigues.

Correct. After the brain has remained active for many hours, neurons in the activating system fatigue, the positive feedback cycle between the mesencephalic reticular nuclei and the cerebral cortex fades, and the sleep-promoting centers of the sleep centers take over, bringing the transition from wakefulness to sleep.

These nuclei drive wakefulness, and it is their fatigue that lets the feedback loop fade. Tell: the centers that take over as the loop weakens are the sleep-promoting centers, which bring the transition into sleep.

The cortex is the partner the reticular nuclei excite in the positive feedback loop that sustains wakefulness. Tell: as that loop fades, control passes to the sleep-promoting centers, not to the cortex.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 19, 18, 10

set1.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set1.q: A 58-year-old man with serious organic brain disease has delta waves on his electroencephalogram. Where in the brain do delta waves arise?
opts: In the thalamus, which drives the cortex

Delta waves persist in the cortex of animals whose cortex has been separated from the thalamus, so the thalamus is not needed for them. Tell: delta waves arise in the cortex itself, independent of lower brain regions.
In the occipital region, as alpha does
The occipital region is where alpha waves are most intense; delta waves are placed in the cortex, independent of lower brain regions, not tied to one lobe. Tell: the occipital link belongs to alpha.

The reticular activating nuclei are the proposed drivers of wakefulness, exciting the cerebral cortex. Tell: delta waves arise in the cortex independent of lower regions of the brain, such as these nuclei.
In the cortex, independent of lower regions

Correct. Delta waves occur strictly in the cortex, independent of activities in lower regions of the brain. They even appear in the cortex of animals whose cerebral cortex has been separated from the thalamus by subcortical transection, so the cortex produces them without input from below.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 26, 22, 18

set1.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set1.q: A 25-year-old man in a sleep laboratory, about 90 minutes after falling asleep and still asleep, shows irregular, high-frequency, low-voltage waves resembling those of an awake person, with bursts of rapid eye movements. Which stage is he in?
opts: Correct. Rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes, and their electroencephalogram is irregular, high frequency and low voltage, similar to wakefulness, with rapid eye movements. A man still asleep 90 minutes into the night with that tracing is in rapid eye movement sleep.

Stage N3 is the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, with large, slow delta waves below 3.5 cycles per second. Tell: his tracing is fast and low voltage, resembling wakefulness, which is the opposite of delta sleep.

Stage N1 is the drowsy transition from wakefulness into light sleep at the start of the night, with theta waves. Tell: 90 minutes in, a waking-like tracing with rapid eye movements marks rapid eye movement sleep instead.

Alert wakefulness shares the fast, irregular tracing, and the two can be hard to tell apart on the electroencephalogram. Tell: he is still asleep, and a waking-like tracing in a sleeper, with rapid eye movements, is rapid eye movement sleep.
ruled out by a stated finding
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 10, 29, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set1.q: A 59-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department unresponsive. She does not open her eyes or move when her name is shouted, when she is shaken, or when firm pressure is applied to her nail bed. Which state best describes her?
opts: Correct. She is unconscious and cannot be aroused by any of the stimuli tried: a shouted name, shaking and painful pressure. Coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused by stimuli, whereas sleep, however deep, is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused.

Stage N3 is the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage and is more difficult to arouse from, but it is still sleep, from which stimuli can arouse a person. Tell: nothing roused her at all, and failure to arouse defines coma rather than any depth of sleep.

Rapid eye movement sleep is a stage of sleep, and people even awaken from it spontaneously in the morning. Tell: she could not be roused by shouting, shaking or pain, so she is not in any stage of sleep; unarousable unconsciousness is coma.

Quiet wakefulness is an awake, relaxed state with alpha waves, the state of someone resting with the eyes closed. Tell: she is unconscious and unresponsive to every stimulus, which rules out any form of wakefulness and fits coma.
ruled out by a stated finding
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 10, 28

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: A 30-year-old resident falls asleep after a 30-hour shift without any sleep. What is expected of the rapid eye movement episodes on her recording tonight?
opts: Rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes within 90- to 120-minute cycles, and extreme sleepiness changes their length, making each one short or even absent. Tell: what sleepiness changes is how long each episode lasts.

Correct. When a person is extremely sleepy, each rapid eye movement episode is short or even absent; as the person becomes more rested, the episodes lengthen. After 30 hours awake she is extremely sleepy, so tonight her rapid eye movement episodes should be brief or missing.

This reverses the pattern: rapid eye movement episodes lengthen as a person becomes more rested and shorten when the person is extremely sleepy. Tell: sleep debt shortens or removes the episodes, and rest lengthens them.
The same as on rested nights

Episode length is not fixed; it depends on how sleepy the person is. Tell: extreme sleepiness makes each rapid eye movement episode short or even absent, so her recording should look different from a rested night's.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 6

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: A 22-year-old woman in a sleep study is in rapid eye movement sleep, with atonia of her voluntary muscles. Which muscles keep working during this atonia?
opts: The eye muscles are spared, and so is the diaphragm, so breathing continues through rapid eye movement sleep, irregular rather than stopped. Tell: the two exceptions to the atonia are the eye muscles and the diaphragm together.

Correct. In rapid eye movement sleep the voluntary muscles are atonic, except the eye muscles and the diaphragm, because alpha motor neurons are inhibited. The spared eye muscles produce the irregular, sharply peaked rapid eye movements, and the spared diaphragm keeps her breathing going, though irregularly.

The limbs are where the atonia shows: voluntary muscle tone is very depressed in rapid eye movement sleep from inhibition of spinal muscle control areas. Tell: the muscles spared from the atonia are the eye muscles and the diaphragm.

The diaphragm is spared, but so are the eye muscles, which is why rapid eye movements can be recorded in this stage at all. Tell: the stage is named for movements of the spared eye muscles, so they cannot be atonic.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 28, 10

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: A 33-year-old man with epilepsy asks why his electroencephalogram looks different from a healthy person's. What determines the intensity and patterns of the electrical activity it records?
opts: The activity of his peripheral nerves

The tracing reflects the level of excitation of different parts of the brain, not peripheral nerves; delta waves, for example, arise in the cortex. Tell: an electroencephalogram records the brain's own electrical activity.
His heart rate and blood pressure

Heart rate and blood pressure change across sleep, falling in non-rapid eye movement sleep, but they are body changes, not the source of the brain's electrical patterns. Tell: the excitation of brain regions determines the tracing.
How excited different brain regions are

Correct. The intensity and patterns of electrical activity on an electroencephalogram are determined by the level of excitation of different parts of the brain, which changes with sleep, wakefulness and brain disorders such as epilepsy or psychosis. His epilepsy alters that excitation, and so his tracing.
Whether he is asleep or awake alone

Sleep and wakefulness do shape the tracing, but brain disorders such as epilepsy or psychosis do too, through the level of excitation of brain regions. Tell: his disorder is itself one of the things that determines the pattern.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 21, 26, 12

set2.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set2.q: A 68-year-old man on a medical ward is found late at night lying still with his eyes closed, not answering when the nurse enters the room. When she calls his name loudly and squeezes his shoulder, he opens his eyes and answers her questions. Which state best explains his earlier unresponsiveness?
opts: Coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused by stimuli. Tell: he opened his eyes and answered once he heard his name and felt the squeeze, so he was arousable, and arousable unconsciousness is sleep, not coma.

Quiet wakefulness is a relaxed, awake state with a decreased level of alertness and alpha waves on the electroencephalogram, not unconsciousness. Tell: he did not answer until he was stimulated, so he was unconscious first, then roused, which is sleep.
ruled out by a stated finding

Alert wakefulness describes a person who is alert, active and processing information, with fast beta waves on the electroencephalogram. Tell: a man lying still who ignores the nurse until he is called loudly and touched is not alert; he was asleep.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. He was unconscious, yet a loud voice and a squeeze of the shoulder roused him and he answered questions. Sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli, which is exactly what happened at his bedside.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 27, 28

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: A 50-year-old man asks whether scientists fully understand why sleep is essential. Which reply is accurate?
opts: No; its functions are still under study

Correct. Sleep has important physiological functions, but researchers have limited understanding of why it is an essential part of life; its specific physiological functions remain a mystery and continue to be researched. Its functions include neural maturation, learning or memory, cognition, waste clearance and energy conservation.
Yes; it exists to save energy

Conservation of metabolic energy is one function among several, and the specific functions of sleep are not settled. Tell: a single settled purpose contradicts the limited understanding researchers describe.
Yes; it mainly rests the muscles

Resting the muscles is not among the functions of sleep; the effects of sleep fall on the nervous system and on the other functional systems, and the specifics remain under research. Tell: the answer to whether it is fully understood is no.
No; it seems to have no real function

Uncertainty about why sleep is essential is not doubt that it matters: sleep has important physiological functions, and restriction over a few days decreases performance and health. Tell: the functions are real; their specifics are still being researched.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 16, 17

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: A 30-year-old woman sits quietly with her eyes closed, relaxed but awake, during an electroencephalogram. The tracing shows rhythmical waves at 10 cycles per second, strongest over the occipital region. Which waveform is this?
opts: Correct. Rhythmical waves at 8 to 13 cycles per second, most intense over the occipital region, are alpha waves. They are found in almost all healthy adults who are awake in a quiet, resting state, such as sitting relaxed with the eyes closed, and they disappear during deep sleep.

Beta waves run faster than 14 cycles per second, are asynchronous and low voltage, and come mainly from the parietal and frontal regions during alert, active thinking. Tell: a rhythmical 10 per second at quiet rest with the eyes closed is alpha.

Theta waves run at 4 to 7 cycles per second and appear in children's parietal and temporal regions, during emotional stress in some adults, and in brain disorders. Tell: 10 per second over the occipital region of a relaxed adult is alpha.

Delta waves run slower than 3.5 cycles per second with high voltage, in very deep sleep, infancy and serious organic brain disease. Tell: she is awake and her rhythm is 10 per second, far faster than delta and inside the alpha range.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 25, 26, 28

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: A 2-month-old boy's parents ask what sleep does for his developing nervous system. Which function of sleep answers them?
opts: This function trims synapses holding unimportant information that might clutter the synaptic network; it is about forgetting, not about maturing. Tell: maturation of a developing nervous system is neural maturation.

Sleep clears metabolic waste generated by neural activity in the awake brain, a cleanup role rather than a developmental one. Tell: the parents ask how sleep helps a nervous system develop, which is neural maturation.

Correct. Neural maturation is one of the functions of sleep, and it is the one that speaks to a developing nervous system. Sleep's physiological effects fall into two groups, effects on the nervous system and effects on the body's other functional systems, and maturation belongs with the first.

Conservation of metabolic energy is a function of sleep, but it concerns energy use rather than development of the nervous system. Tell: the parents ask about a developing nervous system, which is neural maturation.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: A 19-year-old student learning anatomy asks which function of sleep helps her retain what she studies. Which function is it?
opts: Correct. Facilitation of learning or memory is one of the functions of sleep, alongside cognition, and it is the function tied to retaining what she studies. Restricting sleep over a few days lowers cognitive performance, which works against her.

This function works the other way: sleep targets synapses for erasure so that unimportant information that might clutter the synaptic network is forgotten. Tell: erasure helps forget the unimportant, while facilitation of learning or memory helps retain.

Conservation of metabolic energy is a function of sleep, but it concerns the body's energy use, not learning. Tell: holding on to what she studies is the job of the learning or memory function, not of energy conservation.

Sleep clears metabolic waste products generated by neural activity in the awake brain, a housekeeping function rather than one for retaining information. Tell: the function aimed at what she studies is facilitation of learning or memory.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 17, 16

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: A 27-year-old man has had several short nights, and his first recovery night showed short rapid eye movement episodes. He asks what will happen to those episodes as he catches up on sleep. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Shortening goes with greater sleepiness, not with recovery. Tell: as he becomes less sleepy, the duration of each rapid eye movement episode increases, so recovery moves his episodes in the other direction, toward longer ones.
Episode length is not fixed; it rises as sleepiness falls. Tell: his short episodes reflect how sleepy he still is, and they should lengthen as he becomes more rested over the coming nights.

Episodes can be absent when a person is extremely sleepy, which is the state he is leaving behind. Tell: recovery moves him toward longer rapid eye movement episodes, not toward losing them altogether.

Correct. Rapid eye movement episode length follows sleepiness: when a person is extremely sleepy each episode is short or even absent, and as the person becomes more rested (less sleepy), the duration of the episodes increases. Catching up on sleep should lengthen his episodes.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set2.q: A 26-year-old man's sleep recording shows a period of rapid eye movements with atonia of his limb muscles. Which waveform is his electroencephalogram expected to show?
opts: Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep shows beta waves: a mixed, low-voltage, irregular, high-frequency pattern similar to the awake state, but with atonia of the voluntary muscles. His rapid eye movements and limb atonia place him in this stage, also called desynchronized sleep.

Alpha waves mark quiet wakefulness with the eyes closed. Tell: he is asleep with rapid eye movements and limb atonia, a stage whose tracing resembles alert wakefulness, with beta waves rather than the resting alpha rhythm.
Theta waves mark stages N1 and N2 of non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: rapid eye movements with limb atonia mean rapid eye movement sleep, whose tracing is beta-like and similar to the awake state.
Delta waves, slow and high voltage, mark stage N3, the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage. Tell: rapid eye movement sleep has the opposite tracing, fast, irregular and low voltage, with beta waves.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 28, 29, 10

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: A healthy 8-year-old boy has an electroencephalogram while awake. Waves at 5 cycles per second appear over his parietal and temporal regions. Which waveform is this?
opts: Beta waves run faster than 14 cycles per second, are asynchronous and low voltage, and come from the frontal and parietal regions during active thinking. Tell: 5 per second is far slower than beta and falls inside the theta range of 4 to 7.

Delta waves run below 3.5 cycles per second and are typical of infancy and very deep sleep. Tell: he is an awake 8-year-old with a 5-per-second rhythm, inside the theta range of 4 to 7 per second, not the slower delta range.

Correct. Theta waves have frequencies between 4 and 7 cycles per second and occur in the parietal and temporal regions in children. A 5-per-second rhythm over those regions in a healthy 8-year-old is theta, an expected finding at his age rather than a sign of disease.

Alpha waves run at 8 to 13 cycles per second and are most intense over the occipital region of an adult at quiet rest. Tell: 5 per second over the parietal and temporal regions of a child is theta, below the alpha range.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 25, 22, 23, 26

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: A 29-year-old man insists that he never dreams outside the dreaming stage because non-rapid eye movement sleep is dreamless. Which statement about non-rapid eye movement sleep is accurate?
opts: Dreams occur but are often forgotten

Correct. Non-rapid eye movement sleep is often called a dreamless state, but that is not accurate: dreams and nightmares do occur. They are often not remembered because the dreams are not consolidated in memory, and they are less vivid than rapid eye movement dreams.
It is truly a dreamless state

This is the common label, and it is not accurate: dreams and nightmares do occur in non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: they happen but are often not remembered, which is why this sleep only seems dreamless.
Its dreams carry more muscle activity

The reverse is true: dreams during rapid eye movement sleep are the ones associated with more bodily muscle activity. Tell: muscle activity with dreaming points to rapid eye movement sleep, not to non-rapid eye movement sleep.
Its dreams are the most vivid ones

Non-rapid eye movement sleep has less vivid dreams; vivid dreaming is associated with rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: non-rapid eye movement dreams are fainter and often forgotten, while the vivid ones belong to rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 13, 14, 9

set2.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set2.q: A 35-year-old woman is having a routine electroencephalogram. She is alert, chatting with the technician and looking around the room, and the tracing shows fast, low-voltage waves. The technician wants to record her alpha rhythm. What should she be asked to do?
opts: Emotional stress, especially disappointment and frustration, brings theta waves (4 to 7 per second) in some adults, not alpha. Tell: relaxation, not upset, brings out the alpha rhythm of quiet wakefulness.
Close her eyes and rest quietly

Correct. Alpha waves appear when an adult is awake in a quiet, resting state, and closing the eyes in relaxation brings them out, most intensely over the occipital region. Her fast, low-voltage waves are beta waves from alert activity, which give way to alpha once she rests quietly with her eyes closed.

Directing attention to a specific mental activity stops alpha waves and replaces them with beta waves, the opposite of what the technician wants. Tell: alpha needs quiet rest, while focused thinking keeps her in beta.

Alpha waves disappear during deep sleep, where slow delta waves take over. Tell: the alpha rhythm belongs to quiet wakefulness, the relaxed state between alert activity and sleep, so she must stay awake.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 24, 28, 23, 25, 26

set2.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set2.q: A 34-year-old woman lies in bed at lights-out with her eyes closed. Her electroencephalogram shows rhythmical waves at 8 to 13 cycles per second, strongest over the occipital region. Which state does this tracing represent?
opts: Stage N1 is the drowsy transition into light sleep, and its tracing has slowed to theta waves. Tell: a steady, rhythmical 8 to 13 per second over the occipital region is alpha, so she is still awake and resting.

Rapid eye movement sleep shows an irregular, mixed, low-voltage, beta-like tracing with sawtooth waves. Tell: rhythmical alpha at lights-out with closed eyes is quiet wakefulness, well before the first rapid eye movement period about 90 minutes in.

Correct. Rhythmical waves at 8 to 13 cycles per second, strongest over the occipital region, are alpha waves, the mark of quiet wakefulness: an awake person with the eyes closed, relaxed, with a decreased level of alertness. She has not yet fallen asleep.

Alert wakefulness, with the eyes open and the person alert and active, shows beta waves faster than 14 cycles per second. Tell: a rhythmical 8 to 13 per second with the eyes closed is alpha, the relaxed waking state.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 27, 28, 29, 9

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: A 31-year-old man's sleep study shows a mixed, low-voltage electroencephalogram with sawtooth waves, rapid eye movements and atonia of his limb muscles. What explains the atonia?
opts: Increased parasympathetic tone is the autonomic change of non-rapid eye movement sleep, lowering blood pressure, heart rate and breathing. Tell: limb atonia in rapid eye movement sleep comes from inhibited alpha motor neurons, not from autonomic tone.

Fatigue of neurons in the activating system is the proposed reason a person passes from wakefulness into sleep after many hours awake. Tell: it explains falling asleep, whereas atonia within rapid eye movement sleep comes from inhibited spinal motor neurons.

The atonia is not a problem in the muscle itself; it reflects inhibition of the spinal muscle control areas and alpha motor neurons that drive the muscles. Tell: the eye muscles and diaphragm keep working, which exhausted muscles would not explain.

Correct. His tracing, rapid eye movements and atonia place him in rapid eye movement sleep. Muscle tone is very depressed because spinal muscle control areas are inhibited; the inactivity is due to inhibited alpha motor neurons, sparing the eye muscles and the diaphragm.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 28, 14, 19

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: A 26-year-old man is waking up as his sleep centers stop being activated. Which structures are proposed to be released from inhibition and to activate spontaneously?
opts: Sleep-promoting centers within the sleep centers

These take over at the other end of the day, when activating-system neurons fatigue and the feedback cycle fades. Tell: waking begins with the reticular activating nuclei released from inhibition, not with the sleep-promoting centers.
Spinal muscle control areas and motor neurons

Spinal muscle control areas and alpha motor neurons are inhibited in rapid eye movement sleep, producing atonia; they are not the activating system. Tell: waking is driven by the mesencephalic and upper pontile reticular activating nuclei.
Occipital and parietal regions of the cortex

The occipital region is where alpha waves are most intense, and the cortex is the target the reticular nuclei excite, not the source released from inhibition. Tell: release from inhibition happens in the reticular activating nuclei.
Mesencephalic and upper pontile reticular nuclei

Correct. The proposed theory holds that when the sleep centers are not activated, the mesencephalic and upper pontile reticular activating nuclei are released from inhibition and activate spontaneously, exciting the cerebral cortex and peripheral nervous system, which feed back positively to keep them active.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 18, 10, 28, 22

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: A 29-year-old woman's sleep recording shows rapid eye movements, irregular breathing and an electroencephalogram resembling wakefulness. How is her overall brain metabolism expected to change during this period?
opts: A 10 to 30% fall in metabolic rate, along with blood pressure, heart rate and breathing, belongs to non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: her rapid eye movements and waking-like tracing mark rapid eye movement sleep, when brain metabolism rises instead.

Muscle tone is very depressed in rapid eye movement sleep, but that comes from inhibited spinal muscle control areas while the brain itself is very active. Tell: limp limbs and a busy brain go together here, with brain metabolism up by as much as 20%.

The rise is up to 20%, not a doubling or more; 2 to 4 times is the figure for delta wave voltage compared with most other brain waves. Tell: brain metabolism in rapid eye movement sleep climbs by as much as one fifth.

Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep is an active form of sleep in which the brain is very active, and overall brain metabolism can increase by as much as 20% because of that increased brain activity. Her rapid eye movements, irregular breathing and waking-like tracing place her in this stage.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 12, 26

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: A 30-year-old woman wakes in the morning and stays awake through the day without effort. According to the proposed sleep-wake theory, what keeps her wakefulness going once it begins?
opts: Fatigue after many hours awake is what ends wakefulness: the feedback cycle fades and the sleep-promoting centers take over. Tell: fatigue closes the waking day; positive feedback between the reticular nuclei and the cortex carries it.

Increased parasympathetic tone, with low blood pressure and slow heart rate, belongs to non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: it is a feature of sleep, not the loop that sustains wakefulness, which is reticular-cortex positive feedback.

Correct. Once wakefulness begins, it can sustain itself naturally because of a positive feedback mechanism: the reticular activating nuclei excite the cerebral cortex and peripheral nervous system, which send positive feedback signals back to the same nuclei and keep them active.

Wakefulness begins when the sleep centers are not activated, which releases the reticular activating nuclei from inhibition. Tell: active sleep centers would favor sleep, not sustain her waking day; the positive feedback loop does that.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 18, 19, 14

set2.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set2.q: A 66-year-old man in the intensive care unit has been unresponsive for 2 days. His electroencephalogram shows high-voltage waves slower than 3.5 cycles per second, and he cannot be aroused by voice, touch or painful pressure. Which state best describes him?
opts: Alert wakefulness shows fast, low-voltage beta waves in a person who is awake and actively processing information. Tell: he is unresponsive and his waves are slower than 3.5 per second, the opposite of an alert tracing; unarousable unconsciousness is coma.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. The deciding finding is that no stimulus arouses him, which defines coma. His slow, high-voltage delta waves do not decide it on their own, because delta waves occur in very deep sleep as well as in serious organic brain disease; arousability is what separates sleep from coma.

Delta waves do occur in very deep sleep, so his tracing alone could fit it. Tell: a sleeper, however deep, can be aroused by stimuli; he cannot be roused by voice, touch or pain, which makes this coma rather than sleep.
ruled out by a stated finding

Rapid eye movement sleep has an electroencephalogram resembling wakefulness, with irregular, high-frequency, low-voltage waves, not tall, slow delta waves. Tell: his tracing is slow and high-voltage, and no stimulus rouses him, so neither the waves nor the arousal test fit.
ruled out by a stated finding
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 26, 23, 28

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: A 33-year-old woman asks whether the cause of the daily cycle between sleep and wakefulness is fully understood. Which reply is accurate?
opts: Yes; the sleep centers alone control it

The cycle is not settled, and the proposed theory involves the reticular activating nuclei and their positive feedback with the cortex as well as the sleep centers. Tell: there is no definitive explanation, and the theories involve several players.
No; the brain plays no part in it

The proposed theories place the cycle in the brain: the reticular activating nuclei, the cerebral cortex and the sleep centers, and states of brain activity arise from forces generated within the brain. Tell: uncertain does not mean outside the brain.
Yes; it simply follows muscle fatigue

The cycle is not settled, and the fatigue in the proposed theory is of neurons in the activating system, not of muscles. Tell: there is no definitive explanation, and the fatigue that ends wakefulness is neural.

Correct. There is no definitive explanation of the sleep-wakefulness cycle, but there are proposed theories: release of the reticular activating nuclei from inhibition starts wakefulness, positive feedback sustains it, and fatigue of the activating system ends it.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 18, 19, 3

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: A 24-year-old woman's overnight recording is scored stage by stage. About what share of her total sleep time is rapid eye movement sleep expected to fill?
opts: Far too small: rapid eye movement sleep fills about a quarter of a young adult's sleep, with episodes of 5 to 30 minutes recurring about every 90 minutes. Tell: 5 is the shortest episode length in minutes, not the share of the night.

Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep occurs in episodes and occupies about 25% of a young adult's sleep time, and at 24 she is a young adult. The rest of her night is non-rapid eye movement sleep, of which stage N2 is the largest part.

Half would make rapid eye movement sleep as large as all non-rapid eye movement sleep, yet stage N2 alone is the longest stage by total duration. Tell: rapid eye movement sleep is about one quarter of a young adult's sleep.

Three quarters reverses the proportions: most of the night is non-rapid eye movement sleep, with stage N2 the longest stage, and rapid eye movement sleep is about one quarter. Tell: the figure for a young adult is 25%, not 75%.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 13, 28

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: A 2-month-old boy's electroencephalogram shows slow waves below 3.5 cycles per second. Compared with most other types of brain waves, how large is their voltage expected to be?
opts: Low voltage describes beta waves, the asynchronous, fast waves of an alert, actively thinking person, not delta waves. Tell: slow delta waves are the tall ones, often 2 to 4 times the voltage of most other brain waves.

Delta waves stand out by their size: their voltage is often 2 to 4 times greater than that of most other brain waves. Tell: on traces drawn to one voltage scale, the delta trace rises well above the alpha, beta and theta traces.

Correct. Delta waves, which include all waves below 3.5 cycles per second and occur in infancy, often have voltages 2 to 4 times greater than most other types of brain waves. On a tracing they stand out as tall, slow waves, in contrast to the low-voltage beta waves of an alert adult.

This overstates the difference tenfold: delta waves are often 2 to 4 times greater in voltage than most other brain waves. Tell: the multiplier to remember is 2 to 4, not tens of times, for these slow waves of infancy and deep sleep.

set2.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set2.q: A 30-year-old woman in a sleep laboratory, about 40 minutes after falling asleep, shows large, slow waves below 3.5 cycles per second on her electroencephalogram. When the technician calls her name loudly, she wakes and answers. Which state was she in before she woke?
opts: Rapid eye movement sleep shows a mixed, low-voltage tracing with beta waves, similar to the awake state. Tell: large, slow delta waves are the opposite of the fast, desynchronized tracing of rapid eye movement sleep; they mark stage N3.

Correct. Waves below 3.5 cycles per second are delta waves, the wave of stage N3, the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage. That a loud voice woke her confirms sleep rather than coma, because sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by stimuli.

Delta waves also occur with serious organic brain disease, but coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused. Tell: she woke to a loud voice and answered, so her slow waves came from deep sleep, not from coma.

Stage N1 is the drowsy transition from wakefulness into light sleep, with theta waves of 4 to 7 cycles per second. Tell: waves below 3.5 per second are delta waves, which mark the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, not the lightest one.

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: A 4-month-old boy who is feeding well and developing normally has an electroencephalogram showing high-voltage waves below 3.5 cycles per second. Which explanation best fits this finding?
opts: Emotional stress produces theta waves, 4 to 7 cycles per second, in some adults, not delta waves in an infant. Tell: waves below 3.5 per second are delta, and in a thriving 4-month-old, infancy explains them.

Correct. High-voltage waves below 3.5 cycles per second are delta waves, and infancy is one of the settings where delta waves occur, along with very deep sleep and serious organic brain disease. In a healthy infant who is feeding well and developing normally, infancy itself explains them.

Delta waves do occur in persons with serious organic brain disease, but this infant is feeding well and developing normally. Tell: infancy is itself a setting for delta waves, so a healthy baby needs no disease to explain them.
ruled out by a stated finding

Coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused by stimuli, and an infant who is feeding well is plainly arousable. Tell: delta waves in a healthy, feeding infant reflect infancy, not coma.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: A 29-year-old man settles into bed in a sleep laboratory, and a few minutes later he is drowsy and drifting off into light sleep. Which stage is he in?
opts: Stage N3 is the deepest, most restful non-rapid eye movement stage, with delta waves and tissue growth and repair. Tell: he is only drowsy and drifting off, which is the light transition stage, stage N1, not the deepest one.

The first rapid eye movement period comes at the end of the first 90- to 120-minute cycle, after the non-rapid eye movement stages. Tell: a few minutes after lying down he is still in the drowsy transition, stage N1.

Correct. Stage N1 is the transition from wakefulness: the person is somnolent or drowsy and in light sleep. Minutes after settling into bed and drifting off, he fits this first non-rapid eye movement stage, before the deeper stages N2 and N3.

Stage N2 is less responsive, deeper sleep, with heart rate and temperature falling, and it is the longest stage by total duration. Tell: drowsiness at the edge of wakefulness, minutes after lying down, is stage N1.

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: A 31-year-old woman notices that her day moves between focused work, a moment of fear, an evening of exhilaration and then sleep. She asks what generates these different states. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Outside stimuli acting on a passive brain

The states of brain activity arise, for the most part, from forces generated within the brain itself. Tell: the brain is not passive here; its own activating or inhibiting forces produce sleep, wakefulness and mood.

The fatigue in the proposed sleep-wake theory is of neurons in the activating system, not of muscles, and moods such as fear are not explained by muscle signals. Tell: the states come from activating or inhibiting forces within the brain.
Sleep centers that stay switched on

Sleep centers that stay activated would favor sleep, yet she moves through waking states too; wakefulness begins when the sleep centers are not activated. Tell: shifting states come from changing activating or inhibiting forces in the brain.

Correct. The brain has many states of activity, including sleep, wakefulness, extreme excitement and different levels of mood such as exhilaration, depression and fear, and they arise, for the most part, from different activating or inhibiting forces generated within the brain.

set2.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set2.q: A 35-year-old woman lies relaxed with her eyes closed at the start of a sleep study, and her electroencephalogram shows alpha waves. What happens to these alpha waves once she reaches deep sleep?
opts: Tall, high-voltage waves in deep sleep are delta waves, often 2 to 4 times the voltage of other waves; the alpha waves themselves disappear. Tell: the big waves of deep sleep are a different, slower wave, not enlarged alpha.

Beta waves replace alpha when an awake person's attention turns to a specific mental activity. Tell: falling into deep sleep slows the tracing progressively; it does not speed it up into the beta range.

Alpha waves mark quiet wakefulness and disappear during deep sleep. Tell: a persisting alpha rhythm would mean she is still awake and resting quietly, not deeply asleep, since the tracing slows as sleep deepens.

Correct. Alpha waves belong to quiet, relaxed wakefulness, such as resting with the eyes closed, and they disappear during deep sleep. As she sinks into deep non-rapid eye movement sleep the tracing slows progressively, until delta waves below 3.5 cycles per second take over in stage N3.

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: A 45-year-old woman's heart rate and blood pressure fall steadily after she enters non-rapid eye movement sleep. Which autonomic change explains this?
opts: Inhibited spinal muscle control areas and alpha motor neurons explain the atonia of rapid eye movement sleep, a muscle change. Tell: a falling heart rate and blood pressure in non-rapid eye movement sleep are autonomic, from increased parasympathetic tone.

Correct. Non-rapid eye movement sleep brings increased parasympathetic tone, with low blood pressure, slow heart rate and decreased respiratory rate, together with decreased peripheral vascular tone. Her steady fall in heart rate and blood pressure is that parasympathetic shift.

The autonomic change of non-rapid eye movement sleep is increased parasympathetic tone, with low blood pressure and slow heart rate. Tell: her values fall steadily, which matches the parasympathetic change, not a sympathetic one.

This reverses the direction: parasympathetic tone rises in non-rapid eye movement sleep, producing low blood pressure, slow heart rate and decreased respiratory rate. Tell: a falling heart rate and blood pressure go with increased parasympathetic tone.

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: A 27-year-old man's recording, about 90 minutes after he falls asleep, shows irregular, high-frequency waves like those of an awake, active person, while he lies asleep with atonic limbs. Which term names this stage?
opts: Correct. In rapid eye movement sleep the electroencephalogram shows brain wave patterns similar to those during wakefulness, so this stage is also called paradoxical sleep: he is asleep with atonic limbs while his tracing looks awake. Rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes.

Slow-wave sleep is the deep, restful non-rapid eye movement sleep, with slow waves rather than the fast, irregular waves of wakefulness. Tell: a sleeper whose tracing looks awake and active is in paradoxical, rapid eye movement sleep.

Quiet wakefulness is an awake, relaxed state marked by rhythmical alpha waves. Tell: he is asleep, and his waves are irregular and high frequency like those of alert wakefulness, not the steady alpha rhythm of a person resting awake.
ruled out by a stated finding

Stage N1 is the drowsy transition from wakefulness into light sleep, with theta waves. Tell: irregular, high-frequency waves resembling an awake, active person, together with limb atonia 90 minutes into the night, describe rapid eye movement sleep.

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: A 34-year-old new mother has been sleeping about 4 hours a night for a week and has gone back to her office job. Which change is expected from this sleep restriction?
opts: Correct. Sleep restriction over a few days can decrease cognitive and physical performance, overall productivity and the health of a person. A week of about 4 hours a night is restriction over more than a few days, so lower productivity at work is expected.
More output from longer waking days

Extra waking hours do not translate into more output: restriction over a few days decreases overall productivity. Tell: her productivity is expected to fall, along with cognitive and physical performance and health.

This reverses the effect: sleep restriction over a few days decreases physical as well as cognitive performance. Tell: each effect of restriction is a decrease, in performance, productivity and health.
No change for at least a month

Effects appear within days, not after a month: restriction over a few days can decrease performance, productivity and health. Tell: a week of short nights is already longer than the few days that are enough.
